title: Paul's list (2 Corinthians 11:24–28)
hook: beaten, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, and still going

segments.voice: Yesterday, joy in hard times: the apostles left the council rejoicing. Your line was joy anyway. Who did you tell about something you're glad to be part of? Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.

A résumé is a list of wins. Degrees, titles, the big project you led. Nobody puts "was fired twice" at the top. In his second letter to the church in Corinth, Paul is under pressure to produce a résumé. Rival teachers have impressed some in the church, and Paul says he is "not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles." Some readers hear a dry smile in that phrase. So he agrees to boast, and he warns everyone first that he's speaking like a fool. Then he writes a very strange résumé. Today: Paul's list.
screen: `A RÉSUMÉ IS A LIST OF WINS.`

segments.voice: Here is part of it, in the King James words: "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep." He keeps going. Dangers on rivers, from robbers, in the city, in the wilderness, at sea. Then the ordinary misery of travel: "In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness." Read it slowly and it stops sounding like a boast. It sounds like someone emptying his pockets. And look at the last item. After the stonings and the shipwrecks, Paul adds this: "that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches." The final hardship isn't a wound. It's worry. Lying awake over people he loves. He counts that too. Then he tells you why he wrote the list at all: "If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities." Infirmities means weaknesses. And the next story he tells is almost funny. In Damascus the city was guarded to catch him, so he was let down through a window in the wall, in a basket. That's where the chapter ends: a grown man lowered in a basket. Some readers put it this way: the point is not that Paul was tough. The point is that he was still there. Beaten, cold, worried, smuggled out of a city, and still writing to the people he loved, still going.

Here's the practice: list your own survived hardships. Settle, and breathe. Then, quietly, start your own strange résumé. Not the wins. The things you got through. A loss. An illness. A move you didn't want. A year that went wrong. The worry that kept you up at night counts too, just as it did for Paul. Let one come to mind, then another. You don't have to relive them. Just touch each one lightly, like counting on your fingers, and notice that you are here, on the other side of every one so far. If you pray, you can hand the list to God. The bell holds the time.
Paul's list. Beaten, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, worried, and still going. It closes a week that walked through patience, the race, courage, your own story, thanks, and joy in hard times.
Your line: still here. Today, when something feels like too much, remember one thing from your list that once felt like too much, too. Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Christians read Paul's hardship list in 2 Corinthians as a picture of faith that keeps going, and some turn to it in a long, hard season of their own.

fork.setup: you're Paul, in Damascus. the city is guarded to catch you. how do you get out?
options: fight your way through the gate.
get let down through a window in the wall, in a basket.
hide in the city until the guard gives up.
fork.reveal: he's lowered through a window in the wall, in a basket, and escapes. it's how this part of his boast ends: not a victory, a basket.

original.note: Greek: weakness. the King James calls it infirmities in 2 Corinthians 11:30.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of Paul's sufferings to show how tough he was.
what it means: Paul turns a boast upside down. instead of wins, he lists what he got through, worry included.
what a scholar hears: the list sits inside what Paul calls speaking as a fool, an answer to rivals in Corinth, and this part of it ends with an escape in a basket.

notes: 11:24 (the floggings) is in the index range but is not quoted or described in detail, to avoid setting Paul's own people as a foil on a short lesson; Keeper may wish to add it with context.
'The very chiefest apostles' (11:5) is given as Paul's sarcastic name for rivals; the sarcasm is a common reading, not stated in the text. Keeper to confirm.
The Damascus basket (11:32–33) is paraphrased; the text names the governor under King Aretas.
Week-end day: the word segment names the week's days 1408–1413 (patience, the race, courage, making peace with your story, thanks, joy).
Greek ἀσθένεια (11:30 has the genitive plural form); confirm.

Editor pass: 'very chiefest apostles' now quoted from 11:5 with the sarcasm given to 'some readers'; the basket no longer called the end of the whole boast (it continues into chapter 12), only of this list; 'for Christians who read this letter' softened.

Audit (2026-10-02): the teach no longer says the basket "finishes the boast" or ends "this list" (the boast runs on into chapter 12, and the list proper is 11:24–28); now "the next story he tells" and "where the chapter ends".
